html:
The idea that Africans and people of African descent everywhere share a common history and future, and should stand together. It began among Black thinkers in the Americas and the Caribbean in the 1800s and became a driving force of African independence.

Early voices included Edward Wilmot Blyden in Liberia. A Pan-African Conference met in London in 1900, and W. E. B. Du Bois held a series of Pan-African congresses from 1919. Marcus Garvey's mass movement of the 1920s called for Black self-reliance and a return to Africa. Ethiopia, which had beaten Italy at the Battle of Adwa and stayed free, became a symbol, and the Italian invasion of 1935 (Second Italo-Ethiopian War) brought protests across the Black world. The Rastafari movement grew from the same reverence for Ethiopia.

The Manchester congress of 1945 brought together future leaders such as Kwame Nkrumah and Jomo Kenyatta. When Ghana became independent in 1957, Nkrumah said its freedom meant nothing unless all of Africa was free. In 1963 independent states formed the Organisation of African Unity, replaced by the African Union in 2002. Writers such as Cheikh Anta Diop gave the idea a history, and festivals such as FESTAC 77 gave it a stage. The African Continental Free Trade Area is a recent step toward the old dream of unity.
